You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/notes-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/notes-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `text_types`, `dimension_types`, `line_styles`, `units`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type`, `text-type`, `line-style`, `dimension-type`, `filled-region-type`, `fill-pattern`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `normalize_guid`, `find` (an element by id or GUID). `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers with the original's error wording.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type`, `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `lib_name_of`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator — another sub-agent), `slabs::view` (floors, ceilings, roofs, shafts, masses — another), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs, railings — another), `notes::view` (YOURS), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds, done). `schedule/` (another sub-agent) — provides `crate::readers::schedule::field_display(cx, id, field) -> Option<String>` (a field's value as a schedule cell shows it; a stub in your build). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default). `src/styles/` (done by another agent) owns text types, dimension types, line styles, units — read their code for the type definitions and defaults.
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, dimensions, tags, sheets, views… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/notes-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house with dimensions, tags, a note, a spot, a section, elevations, sheets and viewports). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"dimension"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: NOTES — `src/readers/notes/` (`notes::view` for level, grid, dimension, dimension3d, tag, text, spot, section, elevation, sheet, viewport, schedule, view3d, planview, line, region, detailgroup, repeatingdetail, link, cadimport; and the commands `select_by_id`, `ids_of`, `measure`: `notes::cmd_select_by_id`, `cmd_ids_of`, `cmd_measure`)
Every field `elements` shows for these categories, exactly, and the three commands' replies and errors. Observed so far (verify everything and complete):
- level: `computation_height` (1200 unless stored), `view_range`, `extent`, anything else; grid: as stored?
- dimension: `type` (the dimension type's name), `values` (mm), `labels` (the text as drawn, `10300`: with the project's `units` (the `units` command: mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in) and the dimension type's settings — see `src/styles/text.rs` for dimension types), for every `kind` (aligned, linear, angular, radial, diameter, arc_length) and every reference: a wall's centre/left/right faces (`face`; they depend on the wall type's thickness, its location line, flips), start/end, a door's/window's centre and jambs, grids, detail lines, points (`point`, `endpoint`); `dimension_text` (prefix, suffix, above, below, replace), `dimension_constraint` (equal, locked), `dimension_value`, `dimension_3d`.
- tag: `at` (the host's point plus `offset`: a door/window at its point on the host wall, a room at its point, walls, columns, components, floors…), `text` (a door's/window's mark, a room's name, else the type's name; with `label`, the field as its category's schedule shows it → call `crate::readers::schedule::field_display(cx, id, label)` — implemented by the schedule sub-agent; in your build it returns None, so test label tags only for what you can verify and note the rest), `level`, `leader`.
- text: `type` (name), `size` (the text type's), `level` (the view's level, for a note in a plan), notes in sections/elevations/sheets, leaders, runs.
- spot: `elevation` (the height of the top of the host at `at` — a floor's top, a pipe's top…; write your own top-of-host heights for now), `level`; spot_slope's fields.
- section/elevation: `length`, `looking` (the unit vector to the left of start→end), `depth`, crop; note: one elevation's start y came out in `elements` as …1904 where the file had …1902 (`big1.bimcraft`, elevations made by `elevation {}`) — find why (recomputed from something?).
- sheet: `paper` ([420, 297] for A3), `viewports` (their ids); viewport: `size` (the view's extent on paper at its scale: a plan's extent of what it shows (`big1` gives [615.6, 254.4] for Level 1 at 1:100), a section's, an elevation's, a schedule's table size, the 3D view's…), `title` (the view's name).
- view3d (cameras, section boxes, perspective), planview (`duplicate_view`: view_range, dependent views), schedule elements (as stored?), line (detail lines: `length`, `shape`, `style` (name) for lines, arcs, circles, ellipses, splines, polylines, insulation, revision clouds), region (`area_m2`, `type`/`line_style` names, sketch, pattern), detail groups and repeating details (`create_group`, `detail_group`, `repeating_detail`), links (`link`), CAD imports (`import_cad` with a small DXF you write).
- `select_by_id {text}` (ids, GUIDs with/without dashes and braces, IFC GlobalIds, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons, lines: `ids` found, each once, in order; `missing`; `plan` and `extent` [[x, y], [x, y]] — the plan that shows them and where: this needs each element's extent in plan, for every category), `ids_of {ids}` (`id`, `guid`, `ifc` GlobalId — the GUID compressed into IFC's 22-character base64 —, `category`, `name` or type/number/mark), `measure {from, to}` (`length`, `dx`, `dy`, `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise). Match their errors exactly (try every bad input).
Prioritise what typical scripts make (dimensions between walls/grids, tags of doors/windows/rooms, notes, spot elevations on floors, sections, elevations, sheets with plans placed, detail lines) before exotic cases, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call (e.g. a plan-extent function for any element); any edit outside `src/readers/notes/`.

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
Phases: what stood before in halftone, what comes down dashed red, what is new as the category draws it. Phasing: phases in order, and phase filters that say how a view shows each status.
Textures: a material's texture at its real size on the faces it lies on: brick in courses, boards, glass. Paint: a material laid over one face, as Revit's Paint does; Remove Paint takes it off.
Family Editor: parameters, types, forms (extrusions, revolves, voids) and a door's or window's plan symbols, with a preview. Materials: a texture from a pattern or a picture of yours, its tile size, and a favorite kept for every project.
Structure: beams, structural columns, isolated and wall footings and structural floors; Revit's Structure tab on one new element, the run (design). Section: a beam is cut across its section, a round run (a pipe, a steel tube) in a ring.
Beam tool: two clicks, or a chain of them, each step a beam; sketched before the click. Beam properties: heights at both ends, justification, and the system it belongs to.
Pipe tool: two clicks, or a chain; centred on its height by default, falling or rising with a second height. Pipe type: its diameter (or width and depth, if it isn't round) and its material.
Section: a pipe is cut in poché along the line, across it in a ring.
Device tool: the Type Selector lists only the families of its kind; Space turns what you place. Cable tray type: a width by a depth, or round, in a material.
Plumbing: the starter fixtures, a pipe falling to a drain and a riser, in 3D with the walls hidden. Electrical: a tray, a board, luminaires and devices at their mounting heights.
Lightning Protection (SPDA): NBR 5419's vocabulary on the same runs and fixtures; Revit has no such tab. SPDA in 3D: terminals, down conductors and the earthing ring and rods.
Data tab: outlets, a rack, a patch panel and cabling, in NBR 14565's words. Data in 3D: a tray, cables dropping to their outlets, a rack.
## Performance sample Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is [`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder. The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor, and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which. ## Why BIMCraft

  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):

  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.

link :: {path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`

level :: {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid :: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

import_cad :: {path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out

dimension :: {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures

dimension_3d :: {refs: [ref, ref], at: [x, y, z], view?, type?} an aligned dimension in a 3D view (the default 3D view unless `view` names another, by name or id), kept by the view and drawn in it and on a sheet that holds it: how far apart its two references are, along a line through `at` moved square off them. A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. On the desktop, Aligned Dimension (DI) in the 3D view runs it. Returns its id and its length

text :: {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

dimension_constraint :: {id, equal?: bool, locked?: [segment, …]} an aligned or linear dimension's constraints, as Revit's EQ and padlocks: `equal` keeps its segments equal (what it measures to between its first and last moves to keep them so, its ends staying); `locked` lists the segments (counted from 0, west to east or south to north) kept at the lengths they have now. After any command, what a constrained dimension measures to moves with what the command moved, or the command is refused, saying which dimension can't be kept

dimension_text :: {id, segment?, prefix?, suffix?, above?, below?, replace?} a dimension's text, as Revit's Dimension Text: what goes before and after its numbers, over and under them, or in place of them. With `segment` (its numbers counted from 0, west to east or south to north, as `labels` lists them), that one's own, over the dimension's where it says something; an empty text clears it, and a segment with none left goes back to the dimension's

spot :: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up

spot_slope :: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)

tag :: {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

section :: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation :: {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

sheet :: {number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…

place :: {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

crop :: {view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now

duplicate_view :: {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

scale :: {view, scale?: 1 | … | 100000} a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, 1 : `scale`: the paper the view stands for, 1 mm of paper being `scale` mm of the model. Its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, tags, dimension ticks…) and its line weights (pens) are that paper's, so a screen shows them as the paper would at its zoom. Every view has one: 1 : 100 until it is given another, and null is refused. A view placed on a sheet takes it for the viewport's scale. Without `scale` it only says what the view has

dimension_value :: {id, value, segment?} types a length into an aligned or a linear dimension's segment (the first unless told), as a click on its number does: what the segment ends at (its second reference, as the dimension runs west to east or south to north) moves along the dimension so the segment is `value` mm; a locked segment is locked at it, and the other locks hold, or it is refused. Returns {id, moved, by}

filled_region :: {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

create_group :: {ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}

detail_group :: {type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole

repeating_detail :: {type, start: [x,y], end: [x,y], spacing, mirrored?, view?} detail group `type` repeated along the line from `start` to `end`, every `spacing` mm from `start` (at most 2000 of them), each turned along the line, as Revit's Repeating Detail Component: brick coursing, blocking, batt ties. A view draws up to 10000 group members in all (a repeat places each member of the type again), so a type of 100 members repeats up to 100 times. Returns {id, count}

detail_line :: {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

units :: {length?: mm|cm|m|in|ft|ft-in} how drawings, schedules and the desktop show lengths, and read typed ones: millimetres, centimetres, metres, fractional inches, decimal feet, or feet and fractional inches (to 1/16"); areas in m², or ft² with inches and feet. The model, and every command, keep millimetres

schedule :: {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels and masses), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `filters`: [{field, op: equals|not-equals|greater|greater-or-equal|less|less-or-equal|contains|not-contains|begins-with|not-begins-with|ends-with|not-ends-with|has-value|has-no-value, value}, …], the elements all of them keep (text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes or no as no). `sort`: [field or {field, descending?}, …], in turn (its first column unless it says; Phase Created and Phase Demolished in the project's order of phases, a phase never demolished after the last); `grouped`, a row for each set of the sort fields' values: Count and totals summed, and a field whose values differ left empty. Each one given replaces the last; `fields: []` goes back to its category's

section_box :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

perspective :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands

camera :: {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

work_plane :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level

measure :: {from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing

select_by_id :: {text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does

ids_of :: {ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)

elements :: {category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

"""The plan extent (to 0.2 mm) the original gives a set of elements in Level 1's viewport, at 1:1,
found with text-note anchors far away: prints [[minx, miny], [maxx, maxy]] (each to 0.2 mm, rounded up).
usage: vpx.py [-v VIEW] 'cmd' ... """
import sys, subprocess, json
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
a = sys.argv[1:]
view = 'Level 1'
anchor_view = None
cmds = []
while a:
    if a[0] == '-v': view = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    else: cmds.append(a[0]); a = a[1:]
A = 100000
def size(extra):
    allc = cmds + extra + ['sheet {}', 'place ' + json.dumps({'sheet': 'A101', 'view': view, 'scale': 1}), 'elements {"category":"viewport"}']
    args = [ORIG, 'run']
    for c in allc: args += ['--cmd', c]
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, cwd='/tmp/notes-agent/work')
    if p.stderr: print('ERR', p.stderr.decode().strip()); sys.exit(1)
    v = json.loads(p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1])
    return v['elements'][0]['size']
s0 = size([])
lo = size(['text ' + json.dumps({'text': '.', 'at': [A, A], 'view': view})])
hi = size(['text ' + json.dumps({'text': '.', 'at': [-A, -A], 'view': view})])
# with anchor at +A: width = A - minx  (+24)
minx = A - (lo[0] - 24); miny = A - (lo[1] - 24)
maxx = (hi[0] - 24) - A; maxy = (hi[1] - 24) - A
print('size', s0, 'extent', [[round(minx, 3), round(miny, 3)], [round(maxx, 3), round(maxy, 3)]], 'w,h', round(s0[0] - 24, 3), round(s0[1] - 24, 3))

"""Run vpx.py over a list of setups (one per line: commands separated by ' ;; ')."""
import sys, subprocess
for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
    line = line.strip()
    if not line or line.startswith('#'): continue
    view = None
    if line.startswith('@'):
        view, line = line[1:].split(' ', 1)
        view = view.replace('_', ' ')
    cmds = [c.strip() for c in line.split(';;')]
    args = ['python3', '/tmp/notes-agent/vpx.py'] + (['-v', view] if view else []) + cmds
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True)
    print(line[:150], '\n    =>', p.stdout.decode().strip(), p.stderr.decode().strip()[:300])
